title: A Kt/V of 1.08
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; they are not targets. No doses or order sets are given. The unit’s protocol and the attending nephrologist decide every change to the prescription.
intro:
You are the internal medicine resident on the renal rotation, doing the monthly review in a freestanding hemodialysis unit in Angeles City with the fellow, Dr. Carlo Lim. Mrs. Milagros “Mila” Ocampo, 58, a former seamstress with diabetes, dialyzes three times a week, Monday, Wednesday and Friday, for 4 hours, through a tunneled catheter in her right internal jugular vein while she waits for a new fistula. Her dry weight is 65 kg and she passes almost no urine.

This month’s single-pool Kt/V (spKt/V), a measure of urea removal per session, is 1.08; last month it was 1.35. The Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative (KDOQI) 2015 guideline sets a minimum delivered spKt/V of 1.2 for thrice-weekly dialysis.

n1.prompt: What do you do with a spKt/V of 1.08?

choices.text: Nothing. 1.08 is above the KDOQI minimum of 1.0, so the dose is adequate.
choices.feedback: The KDOQI minimum for thrice-weekly dialysis is 1.2 (1B), with a target of 1.4. She is below the floor.
choices.then: Dr. Lim corrects the minimum. You check how the sample was drawn and pull the month’s flow sheets. The post-dialysis sample was drawn correctly. All 12 sessions ran the full 4 hours, but the blood pump ran well below the prescribed speed in most of them, with arterial pressure alarms, and the nurses often reversed the catheter lines.

vitals.pump: Below prescribed speed; arterial alarms; lines often reversed

choices.text: Repeat the Kt/V next week and change nothing until the second result confirms the first.
choices.feedback: Repeating a doubtful sample is reasonable, but the flow sheets already hold the answer. A repeat alone does not tell you whether K, t or V fell.
choices.then: Dr. Lim asks you to review the flow sheets now. The post-dialysis sample was drawn correctly. All 12 sessions ran the full 4 hours, but the blood pump ran well below the prescribed speed in most of them, with arterial pressure alarms, and the lines were often reversed.

vitals.pump: Below prescribed speed; arterial alarms; lines often reversed

choices.text: Before changing anything, check the sample timing and every flow sheet of the month.
choices.feedback: A Kt/V can mislead in either direction: a late sample reads falsely low, a diluted one falsely high. And one full session can hide several short ones, so the flow sheets come first. How and when the post-dialysis sample was drawn; delivered minutes, actual pump speed and alarms.
choices.then: The post-dialysis sample was drawn correctly. All 12 sessions ran the full 4 hours, but the blood pump ran well below the prescribed speed in most of them, with arterial pressure alarms, and the nurses often reversed the catheter lines.

vitals.pump: Below prescribed speed; arterial alarms; lines often reversed

choices.text: Change to a larger dialyzer this week to raise the clearance back above the target.
choices.feedback: A bigger dialyzer raises K only if blood reaches it. Changing the prescription before you know whether K, t or V fell may treat the wrong cause.
choices.then: Dr. Lim holds the change and asks for the flow sheets. The sample was drawn correctly. All 12 sessions ran the full 4 hours, but the blood pump ran well below the prescribed speed in most of them, with arterial pressure alarms, and the lines were often reversed.

vitals.pump: Below prescribed speed; arterial alarms; lines often reversed

n2.prompt: Time was delivered. What do you propose?

choices.text: The catheter cannot deliver the flow: report it for evaluation and push the fistula referral.
choices.feedback: A failing access is the commonest hidden cause of a low dose. The fix for a failing access is not a bigger dialyzer; it is the access. K has fallen because the catheter cannot give the prescribed blood flow, and reversed lines add recirculation; evaluation per unit protocol.

choices.text: Raise the dialysate flow and use a larger dialyzer to make up for the slower blood pump speed.
choices.feedback: Each step gives less than the one before, and neither fixes blood that is not reaching the dialyzer. The cause stays in place.
choices.then: The attending asks for the catheter to be evaluated per unit protocol and the fistula referral to be expedited.

choices.text: Lengthen each session to make up the dose while the catheter stays as it is.
choices.feedback: More time raises t and is a reasonable bridge, but it leaves the failing access unexamined. Find out why K fell.
choices.then: The attending agrees to the longer sessions as a bridge, and asks for the catheter to be evaluated and the fistula referral expedited.

n3.scene: After the catheter is exchanged, the pump runs at the prescribed speed. On Monday, after the weekend, Mrs. Ocampo arrives 3.9 kg above her 65-kg dry weight, with ankle edema but clear lungs. The nurse plans to remove all of it in the usual 4 hours.

choices.text: Remove an extra kilogram today to get ahead of next weekend’s gain.
choices.feedback: Removal beyond refill capacity drops her blood volume, often before the pressure falls. A higher rate means more hypotension and cramps, and cramps shorten sessions.
choices.then: Dr. Lim stops the order. You calculate the rate and discuss the options with him.

vitals.plan: Longer Monday session; salt counseling; dialysate sodium review

choices.text: Her UF rate is 15 mL/kg/h: discuss a longer session, salt, dialysate sodium and dry weight.
choices.feedback: Observational studies associate UF rates above 13 mL/kg/h with higher mortality; they do not prove that lowering the rate saves lives. Over 5 hours the same volume is 12 mL/kg/h, and more time is the lever the module names. 3,900 mL over 4 hours in 65 kg; discuss it with the fellow.

vitals.plan: Longer Monday session; salt counseling; dialysate sodium review

choices.text: Remove only what keeps the rate under 13 mL/kg/h and send her home the rest above dry weight.
choices.feedback: Respecting the speed limit is right, but leaving fluid behind every Monday without a plan builds chronic overload. Add time, sessions or salt work so she can reach dry weight safely.
choices.then: Dr. Lim agrees to cap the rate today and proposes a longer Monday session and salt counseling.

vitals.plan: Longer Monday session; salt counseling; dialysate sodium review

choices.text: Remove all 3.9 kg in 4 hours as usual and treat cramps if they come.
choices.feedback: A rate of 15 mL/kg/h outruns refilling in many patients. Cramps then end sessions early, and the delivered dose falls again.
choices.then: She cramps at hour three and the session ends 30 minutes early. You calculate the rate and discuss it with Dr. Lim.

vitals.plan: Longer Monday session; salt counseling; dialysate sodium review

n4.scene: Her son, a tricycle driver, says the trips are hard: a tricycle and a bus each way, three times a week. He asks whether she could come only twice a week. She passes almost no urine. She was registered in the PhilHealth Dialysis Database (PDD) last year.
n4.prompt: What do you say and do?

choices.text: Agree to twice weekly with longer sessions; transport is a real barrier.
choices.feedback: With almost no urine, twice weekly is underdialysis by arithmetic: the weekly minimum is hard to reach with two sessions, and the long gaps bring bigger gains and higher potassium.
choices.then: Dr. Lim asks you to call the attending and the social worker before anything is changed.

vitals.plan: Stay thrice weekly; social worker for transport; attending informed

choices.text: Tell him the schedule is the attending’s decision and that you will pass the request on.
choices.feedback: Involving the attending is right, but he deserves the reason now, and the barrier he named, transport, can be worked on today.
choices.then: The attending meets the family, explains the reason, and asks the social worker to help with transport.

vitals.plan: Stay thrice weekly; social worker for transport; attending informed

choices.text: Explain why two cannot do the work of three, check the coverage, involve the social worker.
choices.feedback: A family asking to reduce frequency in a patient with little urine is on the module’s stop-and-call list. Twice weekly is a prescription only when residual function is measured and followed; without urine, transport is the problem to solve. Her kidneys no longer help. PhilHealth covers up to 156 sessions a year for PDD patients (confirm on the date of service); the social worker looks at transport; bring the request to the attending.

vitals.plan: Stay thrice weekly; social worker for transport; attending informed

vitals.nutr: Weight down 3 kg; albumin and nPCR falling; poor appetite

n5.scene: In October her spKt/V is 1.55. Her pump runs at the prescribed speed, sessions are full length and her gains are smaller. But she has lost 3 kg of flesh, her appetite is poor, and her albumin and normalized protein catabolic rate (nPCR) are falling.

choices.text: The dose is above target, so the plan is working; recheck the Kt/V next month and keep it.
choices.feedback: The dose is fine, but the number is not the whole story. Falling weight, albumin and nPCR deserve action now.
choices.then: Dr. Lim points to the weight trend and asks for a dietitian review and a dry weight reassessment.

vitals.plan: Dietitian review; dry weight reassessed; look for a cause of poor appetite

choices.text: The Kt/V is well above 1.4, so the sessions can be shortened.
choices.feedback: Part of that rise may be a shrinking V, not better dialysis. Cutting time would lower clearance in a patient who is already losing weight, and time also removes phosphate and water.
choices.then: Dr. Lim declines and asks for a dietitian review and a dry weight reassessment.

vitals.plan: Dietitian review; dry weight reassessed; look for a cause of poor appetite

choices.text: A smaller V from muscle loss may explain it: ask about intake, dietitian, dry weight, attending.
choices.feedback: Muscle wasting lowers V, so the same Kt gives a higher Kt/V, a reassuring number in a malnourished patient. A falling nPCR with a “good” Kt/V is the warning that V, not K, has changed. Refer to the dietitian, reassess her dry weight as she loses flesh, and look for a cause with the attending.

vitals.plan: Dietitian review; dry weight reassessed; look for a cause of poor appetite

end.title: December
end.text: Her new fistula is in use. With dietitian support her appetite and weight are recovering, her dry weight has been reset, and her spKt/V is above target on a measured, full-length, thrice-weekly schedule. The social worker found a neighbor with a tricycle who takes her for a fixed fare.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Check the measurement and the month, not one number: sample timing and technique, delivered minutes, actual pump speed.
  • Ask which of K, t or V explains a low Kt/V before changing anything; a failing access is fixed at the access, not with a bigger dialyzer.
  • Turn every weight gain into a UF rate. Above about 13 mL/kg/h, the levers are more time, more sessions and less salt.
  • Twice weekly without urine is underdialysis. Use the PhilHealth benefit, solve transport, and bring the request to the attending.
  • A high Kt/V in a shrinking patient may mean a smaller V; watch weight, albumin and nPCR.

See Kinetics, UF and dry weight and HDF and incremental HD.
